title: Pointers
summary: A **pointer** is a variable that stores a **memory address**. `&x` gives the address of `x`. `*ptr` follows the address to the value. Unlike a reference, a pointer can be `nullptr` and can be aimed at something else.
markdown:
## A variable that holds an address Every variable lives at an address in memory ([[2.01 Memory, Bits and Fundamental Types]]). A pointer stores one of those addresses. ```cpp int x{ 42 }; int* ptr{ &x }; // ptr holds the address of x ``` ``` ptr x ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │ 0x7ff0 ──┼───────────▶ │ 42 │ └────────────┘ └────────────┘ lives at 0x7ff8 lives at 0x7ff0 ``` | Expression | Meaning | Value here | |---|---|---| | `x` | The value of `x` | `42` | | `&x` | The address of `x` | `0x7ff0` | | `ptr` | The address stored in `ptr` | `0x7ff0` | | `*ptr` | The value at that address | `42` | | `&ptr` | The address of the pointer itself | `0x7ff8` | Following a pointer to the thing it points at is called **dereferencing**. ```cpp *ptr = 100; // change x through the pointer std::cout << x << '\n'; // 100 ``` > [!info] `*` and `&` each have two meanings > | Symbol | In a declaration | In an expression | > |---|---|---| > | `*` | `int* p`: `p` is a pointer to `int` | `*p`: dereference `p` | > | `&` | `int& r`: `r` is a reference to `int` | `&x`: the address of `x` | ## Aiming a pointer somewhere else ```cpp #include int main() { int a{ 1 }; int b{ 2 }; int* p{ &a }; std::cout << *p << '\n'; // 1 p = &b; // p now points at b std::cout << *p << '\n'; // 2 return 0; } ``` Assigning to `p` changes **where it points**. Assigning to `*p` changes **the thing it points at**. Keep those two apart and pointers stop being confusing. ## `nullptr`: pointing at nothing A pointer can deliberately point at nothing. That value is `nullptr`. ```cpp int* p{ nullptr }; if (p != nullptr) { std::cout << *p << '\n'; } else { std::cout << "no value\n"; } ``` A pointer converts to `false` when it is null, so `if (p)` means the same as `if (p != nullptr)`. > [!danger] Dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behaviour > In practice the program usually crashes with an *access violation*. Whenever a pointer might be null, test it before you dereference it. ## Passing an address to a function ```cpp void reset(int* p) { if (p) { *p = 0; } } int score{ 99 }; reset(&score); // the & at the call shows that score may be changed reset(nullptr); // allowed: "there is nothing to reset" ``` A pointer parameter can express "there might be no object". A reference parameter cannot. ## Pointers and `const` `const` can apply to the thing pointed at, to the pointer itself, or to both. Read the declaration from right to left. | Declaration | Read as | Change the value through it? | Aim it elsewhere? | |---|---|---|---| | `const int* p` | pointer to const int | No | Yes | | `int* const p` | const pointer to int | Yes | No | | `const int* const p` | const pointer to const int | No | No | The first is by far the most common. It means "I will look, but not touch", exactly like a const reference. ## Pointers to structs: `->` To reach a member through a pointer, use `->`. ```cpp struct Point { int x{}; int y{}; }; Point pt{ 3, 4 }; Point* pp{ &pt }; std::cout << (*pp).x << '\n'; // 3: dereference, then take the member std::cout << pp->x << '\n'; // 3: the same thing, written the usual way ``` ## Pointer or reference? | | Reference `T&` | Pointer `T*` | |---|---|---| | Can be null | No | Yes | | Can be aimed elsewhere | No | Yes | | Must be initialized | Yes | No, but always do it | | Used like | The variable itself | `*p` and `p->` | ```mermaid flowchart TD Q{"Might there be no object,
or must it change target?"} -- no --> R["Use a reference"] Q -- yes --> P["Use a pointer"] ``` Use a reference unless you need one of the two things only a pointer can do. Pointers become essential with dynamic memory: [[7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory]]. ## Dangling pointers Like a reference, a pointer can outlive its target. ```cpp int* p{}; { int temp{ 5 }; p = &temp; } // temp is destroyed here *p = 1; // undefined behaviour: p is dangling ``` Nothing sets `p` to null for you. It still holds the old address, and that memory may now be used for something else. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? After `int* p{ &x }; *p = 7;`, what is `x`? - Unchanged - The address 7 + `7` - Undefined, because `p` was never initialized > `*p` is the variable `p` points at, so assigning through it changes `x` to 7. ? What is the difference between `const int* p` and `int* const p`? + The first cannot change the value it points at; the second cannot be aimed at a different address - The first cannot be aimed elsewhere; the second cannot change the value - There is none; the `const` can go on either side - The first points at a constant; the second is not allowed > Read right to left: `const int*` is a pointer to a const int; `int* const` is a const pointer to an int. ? When would you choose a pointer over a reference? - Always, because pointers are faster - Whenever the function only reads the value it is given + When it may point at nothing, or at different objects over time - Whenever the value is an `int` > A pointer can be `nullptr` and can be re-aimed. When neither is needed, a reference is simpler and safer. ? What is the difference between `p = &b;` and `*p = b;`? - There is none - The first copies `b`'s value; the second makes `p` point at `b` - Both make `p` point at `b`; the second also copies its value + The first makes `p` point at `b`; the second copies `b`'s value into whatever `p` points at > Without `*` you change the pointer itself. With `*` you change the object it points at. ```
ideas:
1. For some `int x` and a pointer to it, print `x`, `&x`, `ptr`, `*ptr` and `&ptr`.
2. Write `void swapByPointer(int* a, int* b)` and compare it with the reference version from the last lesson.
3. Write `const int* findLarger(const int* a, const int* b)` that returns `nullptr` if either argument is null.

cards.a:
`7`

`*p` is the variable `p` points at, so assigning through it changes `x` to 7.

cards.q: What is the difference between `const int* p` and `int* const p`?
cards.a:
The first cannot change the value it points at; the second cannot be aimed at a different address

Read right to left: `const int*` is a pointer to a const int; `int* const` is a const pointer to an int.

cards.q: When would you choose a pointer over a reference?
cards.a:
When it may point at nothing, or at different objects over time

A pointer can be `nullptr` and can be re-aimed. When neither is needed, a reference is simpler and safer.

cards.q: What is the difference between `p = &b;` and `*p = b;`?
cards.a:
The first makes `p` point at `b`; the second copies `b`'s value into whatever `p` points at

Without `*` you change the pointer itself. With `*` you change the object it points at.
